title: Property Management Keywords: The Complete SEO Guide
content:
| Tier | Keyword tier | Conversion / audience notes |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | Near-me and high-volume head terms | High search volume; primarily driven by the Google Business Profile (GBP) Map Pack. Searches often come from property owners beginning their search. |
| T2 | Service + location terms | **Highest converting for owner acquisition.** Searchers are property owners actively choosing a local provider; the page says these terms “actually fill your management portfolio.” |
| T3 | Property type keywords | Target landlords searching for management of a specific property type; the page recommends one dedicated page per type. |
| T4 | Pricing and fees keywords | Vendor due-diligence searches that convert extremely well; searchers may be close to hiring and comparing providers. |
| T5 | Informational and question keywords | Reach landlords in the research stage and build trust before they contact a company. |
| T6 | Service-specific keywords | Reach landlords seeking a particular service; the page says these convert at high rates because intent is specific. |
| T7 | Tenant search keywords | Secondary audience for filling vacancies. Broad terms are portal-dominated; niche and hyper-local searches are more viable. |

title: Property Management Marketing Plan for Google Search Ads
content:
## Owner search volumes by buyer stage

US monthly search volumes are from Google Keyword Planner.

| Buyer stage | Search keyword | Monthly searches |
|---|---|---:|
| Unaware | “how to rent out a house” | 4,400 |
| Unaware | “renting out my house” | 480 |
| Unaware | “should i rent or sell my house” | 390 |
| Problem aware | “How to evict a tenant” | 720 |
| Problem aware | “tenant not paying rent” | 260 |
| Problem aware | “how to screen tenants” | 170 |
| Solution aware | “How much does property management cost” | 2,900 |
| Solution aware | “property management fees” | 2,900 |
| Solution aware | “what does a property manager do” | 2,900 |
| Solution aware | “is a property manager worth it” | 140 |
| Solution aware | “should i hire a property manager” | 30 |
| Service aware | “Property management company” | 49,500 |
| Service aware | “property management near me” | 40,500 |
| Service aware | “property management companies near me” | 18,100 |
| Service aware | “rental property management” | 12,100 |
| Most aware | Searches for the company’s name, often with “reviews” or “fees” | Not stated |

- The four service-aware searches total about **120,000 US searches per month**.
- The article says early-stage searches total about **15,000 per month**, roughly one-eighth the service-aware volume.
- “Property management near me” has **40,500 searches a month**; “should i hire a property manager” has **30**.

### Example local-market volumes: Orlando area

| Search keyword | Monthly searches |
|---|---:|
| “property management near me” | About 590 |
| “property management company” | About 590 |
| “property management orlando” | About 390 |

The page says problem-stage searches checked in the Orlando example barely registered. It does not provide their individual volumes.

## Buyer-stage guidance

| Stage | What the owner is doing, as described |
|---|---|
| Unaware | Owns a property but does not think they need a manager; searches for the job of renting out the property. |
| Problem aware | Has encountered a problem, such as an eviction or unpaid rent, but is still trying to handle it themselves. |
| Solution aware | Knows managers exist and is weighing the cost or whether hiring one is worthwhile. |
| Service aware | Has decided to hire and is looking for a company. |
| Most aware | Already has a company on their shortlist and searches for its name, often adding “reviews” or “fees.” |

The article says Google Ads is best suited to the last two jobs—getting considered and chosen—and describes a paid click as expensive education for an owner who is not ready to hire.

## Recommended ad structure

| Phase or campaign type | Recommended use and details |
|---|---|
| **Search — start here** | Target service-aware searches first. Begin with exact-match keywords and bids set by hand. The article calls this opening campaign **“Isolation”**—BrandRocket’s own term, not a Google setting. |
| **Broader matching — later** | BrandRocket calls this **“Exploration.”** Wait until the account logs about **30 quality owner leads per month** before expanding matching. |
| **Performance Max — later** | It spreads one budget across Search, Maps, Gmail, Discover, Display, and YouTube. The article recommends adding it later, once the account is sending enough quality leads for it to learn from. |
| **Demand Gen — later** | Shows ads on YouTube, Gmail, Discover, and Display sites to reach owners before they search; the article identifies it as a channel for problem-aware owners. Google wants a Demand Gen budget of **10 times the target cost per lead or more**. The page characterizes that as a large amount at an owner lead’s price. |
| **Display** | The page says Display, which once ran on its own, now sits inside Demand Gen. |

The article gives **months two to three and six to seven** as the usual pace for later steps, but says this is not a rule: a larger account that reaches the lead threshold sooner can move sooner. Its recommended order is Search first, then broader matching, then Performance Max and Demand Gen.

## CPC, bids, and cost-per-lead information

| Item | Amount or detail |
|---|---|
| High-end top-of-page bid for the three biggest service-aware searches nationally | About **$14–$17**. The page does not identify which three searches it means in this bid statement. |
| High-end top-of-page bid for “how to rent out a house” | Near **$16**. |
| Demand Gen budget guidance | **10 times the target cost per lead or more**. |
| Actual owner cost per lead | **Not stated.** |
| Actual paid CPCs | **Not stated**; the figures given are high-end top-of-page bid estimates. |

The article says the high-end bids for the biggest service-aware searches are close to the bid for “how to rent out a house,” despite the difference in buyer readiness.

## Other owner-search data

| Data point | Figure or detail |
|---|---|
| Owner-search seasonality, last 12 months across nine owner-side searches (100 = average month) | January: **122**; October: **123**; May through August: **80–86**. |
| Longer-term owner-search pattern | A four-year view of core owner searches is described as noisier, with a few one-off spikes; January stayed well above average in every view the authors pulled. |
| Referral and growth tactics | A 2027 Buildium and NARPM industry-report survey of more than **930** property managers found **53%** of growing companies named referrals from owner clients among their top three growth tactics, **40%** named referrals from other professionals, and **18%** named more marketing and advertising. |
| Owner/board-member discussion of finding or vetting managers | In **24 Reddit threads**, the article counted: interviewing several firms **44** times; referrals **31**; firm size or doors per manager **25**; online reviews **21**; Google search **4** times.

title: Property Management Lead Generation With Manual Google Ads
content:
## Cost per owner lead

| Figure | Details |
|---|---|
| **$109–$459 per owner lead** | Estimated from Orlando top-of-page bids of about **$4.04–$17.00** for “property management near me,” using a **3.70% conversion rate**—the real-estate benchmark published by WordStream. The page says that benchmark is for a broad category that includes agents. |
| **$3,270–$13,770 per month for 30 owner leads** | Arithmetic using the $109–$459 cost range. The chapter headline rounds this to **$3,300–$13,800**. |
| **About $300 per owner lead** | An agency selling Google Ads to property managers gives this as its own average; the page identifies it as the agency’s claim, not an audited measurement. |
| **About $1,000 per month for two to five owner leads** | The same agency suggests this as a “realistic” budget to start to “expect” that lead volume. The page characterizes this as the agency’s sales pitch, not a measurement, and says owner leads at this budget come in single digits each month. |

**Owner-lead-to-signed-client conversion rate:** The page does not state a rate for converting owner leads into signed clients or signed doors. The **3.70%** figure is a lead conversion rate used to estimate cost per lead; it is not a lead-to-signed-client rate.

## Campaign recommendations

- **Keep the owner campaign on manual bids while owner leads are below about 30 quality leads per month.** The page says most property management accounts do not reach that volume, and manual bidding may remain appropriate for as long as the campaign runs.
- **Use Manual CPC** to cap the price of an individual owner click. Give each owner ad group one bid, assigning a separate bid to a keyword only when its performance differs from the group.
- **Start bids near the top of Keyword Planner’s range** for the first few weeks, then gradually lower bids as click and quality data accumulates, while keeping ads near the top.
- **Use a hand-bid, exact-match owner campaign called Isolation** to protect searches known to produce owner leads.
- **Check performance weekly:** top impression share, lost top impression share by rank or budget, Auction Insights, and keyword-level Quality Score readings. The page says to aim for top ads on owner keywords that bring signed doors roughly **75%–90% of the time**.
- **Address the cause of lost impression share:** improve the ad or landing page, or raise the bid when loss is due to rank; add budget or cut weak keywords when loss is due to budget. The page cautions that a higher bid will only drain the budget sooner when the campaign is budget-limited.
- **Use Auction Insights to decide where to compete.** If a rival drives an owner-search price above what a door earns, let that search go and put budget into searches that can be held profitably.
- **Fix ad or landing-page issues before raising bids** when Quality Score is weak. Improve ad relevance or move the keyword to a better group; direct ads to the owner page rather than the home page if the landing-page experience is weak.
- **Move to Target CPA only after the account has about 30 quality owner leads per month.** Create a broad-match sibling campaign called Exploration using Isolation’s best keywords, and set its target from Isolation’s actual cost per owner lead. The page says Google recommends evaluating performance on at least **30 conversions** and cautions that an overly ambitious target can cost conversions.
- **Verify that reported leads are genuine owner leads.** Review a sample of ad calls weekly; tenant, vendor, or job-seeker calls can be counted as owner leads if tracking does not distinguish them. The page recommends correcting tracking and using owner-only form answers, call review, and negative keywords rather than adjusting bids based on an unreliable lead count.
- **Keep owner and leasing campaigns separate, with separate conversion goals.** Leasing campaigns can move to Target CPA once tour requests reach about **30 per month**; the page says leasing campaigns often reach that volume before owner campaigns.
- **Leasing lead-cost context:** the page reports one apartment marketing agency’s target of **about $46–$60 per renter lead** and another’s claimed industry average of **near $70**. It contrasts these with the roughly **$300 owner-lead** figure and says these renter-lead figures are agency targets or claims, not audited numbers.

title: How Rental Owners Evaluate a Property Manager
content:
## Survey context

- Buildium’s 2026 Rental Owners’ Survey included **300 U.S. rental property owners with small portfolios**; **95% owned 1–20 units**.
- The survey was fielded in **February and March 2026**. The article also describes it as gathering owners’ thoughts in March.
- Only **23%** of rental owners said their property manager delivers **excellent value** in 2026.

## What owners value when choosing a property manager

| Priority | Owners selecting it |
|---|---:|
| Tenant management | 57% |
| Maintenance coordination | 43% |
| Customer service | 34% |
| Responsiveness | 31% |

- Owners value maintenance/repairs as the most valuable service their property manager provides: **59%**.
- Maintenance was the primary stressor for **46%** of owners in 2026, making it their top source of stress. The article says maintenance has ranked as their #1 source of stress since Buildium began measuring it in 2018.
- **55%** of owners do not live near their properties.
- In tenant management, owners care most about vacancies being filled quickly, rents being collected on time, and high-quality residents being retained from year to year.
- **36%** of owners said they planned to raise rents to market rate in 2026, down **15 percentage points** from the previous year.

## How owners evaluate manager performance

| Performance measure | Owners identifying it |
|---|---:|
| Response time | 43% |
| Maintenance turnaround | 31% |
| Occupancy rate | 30% |
| Time to lease | 25% |

- Response time is described as the **single most important criterion** owners monitor when evaluating a property management company.
- Owners evaluate managers primarily on speed and execution, including response time and maintenance turnaround.
- The article describes the main evaluation factors as tenant outcomes, maintenance execution, communication speed, financial control, and access to clear reporting.
- Owners judge tenant-related performance through vacancies, collections, and resident retention.
- Owners want clear reporting and self-service access to information, documentation, and reporting. One owner specifically requested monthly rent collected by property, amounts tenants are behind, and transparent information about repairs, vacancies, and tenant issues, accessible through a portfolio dashboard.

## Why owners switch or consider switching managers

| Reason for switching | Owners identifying it |
|---|---:|
| Poor communication | 57% |
| Declines in service quality | 54% |
| Lack of transparency | 34% |

- Poor communication is the **#1 reason** owners switch property managers and the #1 mistake that would prompt them to look for a new management company.
- Owners also cited unexpected fees, lack of transparency, and declines in customer service as conditions that prompt them to reconsider working with a manager.
- Unexpected maintenance costs and maintenance cost surprises can damage owners’ perception of value. The article says poor responsiveness and maintenance cost surprises are especially likely to drive churn.
- Owners identified responsiveness and transparency as areas where their property management company had the most room to improve.
- One owner said that an absence of communication leads them to assume nothing is being actioned.

## Communication expectations

- Owners generally prefer **low-frequency communication** and monthly non-urgent updates.
- **39% of Accidental Landlords** want to hear from their manager only as needed.
- When owners have a question or an issue arises:
  - **43%** expect a same-day response.
  - **42%** expect a response by the next business day.
- The article says owners expect a response by the next business day at the latest. Acknowledging receipt and saying that the manager is working on a solution can help extend an owner’s patience.
- Owners prefer fewer non-urgent updates but expect fast responses when issues arise.
- The article characterizes the desired experience as **low-noise, high-reliability** and says silence when issues arise rapidly erodes trust.

## Decisions and approvals owners want to control

- **50%** of owners want to be consulted before decisions about selecting new tenants, increasing rent, or offering concessions.
- **84%** want to approve large-ticket repairs before the work is completed.
- Owners want an opportunity to weigh in on large repairs and renovations, tenant selection, and rent increases or decreases.
- Owners of all kinds want to stay apprised of rent changes; Accidental Landlords particularly like to be involved in tenant selection.
- Owners want managers to operate independently within clearly defined boundaries, particularly where financial risk is involved. The article says clear approval thresholds and workflows, proactive communication, and transparency around financial decisions matter to owner satisfaction and retention.

title: Website conversion benchmarks for property managers
content:
## Website conversion rate benchmarks

| Performance category | Conversion rate | Characteristics |
|---|---:|---|
| Underperforming | Below 1% | Weak calls-to-action; generic messaging; poor mobile experience; limited trust signals; slow lead-response processes |
| Average-performing | Between 1% and 3% | Basic lead-capture forms; clear service pages; moderate search visibility; functional mobile experience |
| High-performing | Above 3% | Strong owner-focused messaging; multiple lead-capture opportunities; strategic trust indicators; mobile-first design; integrated marketing and follow-up systems |

The page says there is no universal benchmark because traffic quality, market competition, and lead sources vary. Its FAQ says many property management websites convert between 1% and 3%, while high-performing websites often exceed 3%.

## Recommended page elements and supporting features

- **Strong, clear calls-to-action** and owner-focused messaging.
- **Lead-capture forms** that collect enough information for meaningful conversations without unnecessary barriers; avoid excessive form fields.
- **Rental analysis tools** that provide immediate, personalized value while capturing lead information.
- **Owner-focused landing pages** and clear service pages.
- **Live chat and messaging** for visitors who have questions before scheduling a consultation.
- **Online scheduling** to encourage inquiries and consultations.
- **Trust and social-proof elements**, including client reviews, testimonials, case studies, and local success stories.
- **Strategically placed contact information** that is easy to find.
- **Mobile-first design** and good mobile usability.
- **Fast page speeds** and uncluttered navigation.
- **Website integrations**, including:
  - CRM systems
  - Property management software
  - Lead-routing systems
  - Marketing automation tools
  - Reporting and analytics platforms
- **Call tracking and analytics** to monitor traffic and conversions and identify improvement opportunities.
- **Efficient lead follow-up processes** connected to the website and business operations.

title: Property Management SEO: Get More Qualified Owner Leads
content:
## Goodjuju 2026 property management lead-source study

| Finding | Reported figure |
|---|---:|
| Property management companies compared | 35 |
| Measurement periods | Spring and fall |
| Visitors in the fall analysis | 141,908 |
| Owner leads in the fall analysis | 1,262 |
| Share of owner leads attributed to Google Search and the Map Pack | 50.6% |
| Share of owner leads attributed to AI tools | 3.4% |
| Share of website traffic attributed to AI tools | 0.8% |
| Conversion rate for AI-referred visitors | 3.9% |
| Conversion rate for Google Search and Map Pack visitors | 1.2% |

- **Source:** Goodjuju, “2026 property management lead source study.”
- **Caveats stated in the page:** The findings come from one agency’s client sample; the participating businesses worked with the same marketing agency, so the results are not universal industry benchmarks. The lead figures count owner form submissions, not every phone call or enquiry.
- The page provides figures for Google Search and the Map Pack, and AI tools; it does not give a complete ranking of all lead sources.

## Other reported statistics and sources

### Clienvora property management website audit

The audit covered **111 US property management websites** across **10 metros**—Austin, Phoenix, Atlanta, Tampa, Dallas, Miami, Charlotte, Denver, Nashville, and Las Vegas—and was conducted on **November 4, 2026**.

| Audit finding | Result |
|---|---:|
| Published a specific management fee | 25 of 111 (22.5%) |
| Had three or more city-level pages | 88 of 111 (79.3%) |
| Used LocalBusiness or equivalent schema | 65 of 111 (58.6%) |
| Used FAQPage schema | 8 of 111 (7.2%) |
| Blocked at least one AI crawler | 6 of 111 (5.4%) |
| Had an enquiry form asking how many units the owner manages | 0 of 59 (0%) |
| Blocked GPTBot | 5 of 111 (4.5%) |
| Published an `llms.txt` file | 47 of 111 (42.3%) |
| Median number of city-level URLs per site | 5 |

- The audit counted a fee only when it appeared in visible text with a number.
- **Source:** Clienvora’s audit and dataset, as described in the page.

### Other figures in the article

| Figure | Context and qualification |
|---|---|
| 500 organic visitors, 20 owner enquiries, 5 qualified prospects, 1 signed management agreement | Illustrative monthly funnel, not an industry average. The page’s example assumes a 4% visitor-to-enquiry rate, a 25% enquiry qualification rate, and a 20% qualified-prospect-to-client rate. |

title: How Much Does Property Management Cost in Denver? (2026 Guide ...
content:
## Typical Denver management fee

- Management companies typically charge **8–12% of collected rent**. The advertised national average is about **8.5%**.
- Denver’s median asking rent is about **$1,910 per month** (Zillow Observed Rent Index, May 2026, Denver metro area).
- At that rent, the management percentage alone is approximately:
  - **8%:** $1,834 per unit per year
  - **10%:** $2,292 per unit per year
  - **12%:** $2,750 per unit per year
- The page says individual Denver firms may quote above or below the national percentage range. Add-on fees come on top of the monthly percentage.

## Add-on fees

| Fee | Typical amount stated | Details |
|---|---:|---|
| Tenant placement / leasing | **50–100% of the first month’s rent** | Charged each time a new tenant is placed. Covers marketing, showings, screening, lease preparation, and move-in. iPropertyManagement’s measured average is **70.6% of one month’s rent** when bundled with management and **81.8%** for placement-only. Flat-rate alternatives average **$555.53** with management and **$670.23** for placement-only. The page describes this as the biggest add-on and says it recurs with each turnover. |
| Lease renewal | **$200–$500 flat** | Charged when an existing tenant re-signs, often annually. iPropertyManagement’s measured average is **$211.92**. Baselane cites **$100–$300** or a percentage of one month’s rent. |
| Maintenance markup / coordination | **Most-cited range: 10–15% added to vendor invoices; sources span 5–25%** | A surcharge for coordinating a vendor, in addition to the repair bill. On **$3,000 per year** of repairs, a **15%** markup is **$450 per year**. Some firms instead use in-house crews at above-market hourly rates. |
| Vacancy | **$50–$150 per month** while the unit is empty | Some contracts charge an amount equivalent to one month’s rent or continue billing the full management fee under “rent due” contracts. The fee is for overseeing an empty unit, including inspections, lawn care, and marketing. The page advises checking whether management fees are charged on **rent collected** or **rent due**; the latter means fees continue during vacancy. |
| Setup / onboarding | **$200–$500 one-time per property** | Most sources cluster at **$300–$500**. May cover bookkeeping setup, an initial inspection, and registration help; charged before the PM has collected rent. |
| Eviction coordination | **$200–$500 for the PM’s time** | DoorLoop cites **$300–$1,000+**. Court filing fees and attorney costs are billed to the owner in addition to the PM fee. Covers serving notices, court appearances, and coordinating turnover. |
| Early termination | **$50–$1,000 flat**, or roughly **one month’s management fee or more** | Some contracts demand all remaining management fees for the contract term. Contracts typically require **30–60 days’ notice**; some allow the PM to hold owner funds, including the reserve, for **30–60 days** after termination to cover trailing expenses. |
| Inspection | **$75–$300 per inspection** | iPropertyManagement’s measured average is **$106.72**. Move-in/move-out inspections are often bundled; periodic or extra inspections, such as drive-bys or annual interior inspections, are frequently billed separately per visit. |

## All-in cost estimates and examples stated on the page

- Industry blog analyses cited on the page describe the monthly management fee as one of **5–8 fees** managers commonly charge. They say total **first-year costs typically run 18–20% of gross rent**, and recommend budgeting **12–15% of gross rent** even when the base rate is **8–10%**, because lease-up fees, maintenance markups, and miscellaneous charges can add roughly **3–5 percentage points** to the effective rate.
- The page characterizes these as practitioner/blog estimates, not government statistics, and says to present them as **“typically 12–20% all-in, first year highest.”**
- Worked example from those sources: at **$2,000 per month** rent and a **10%** management fee:
  - Base fee: **$2,400 per year**
  - Amortized lease-up: **$750 per year** (0.5 turnovers × $1,500)
  - Maintenance markup: **$450 per year** ($3,000 in repairs × 15%)
  - Total: **$3,600 per year**, or an effective **15% of gross rent**
- The page says turnover frequency is the biggest swing factor: a placement fee of **70–100% of one month’s rent** equals **6–8% of a full year’s gross rent** by itself in a turnover year.
- First-year example for one Denver rental at **$1,910 per month**, with a new management contract and one tenant placed:
  - Management fee at 10%: about **$2,292**
  - Placement fee at 70.6% of one month’s rent: about **$1,348**
  - Setup fee: about **$350**
  - First-year total: about **$3,990**, or roughly **17.4% of gross rent**
  - Excludes maintenance markups, later-year renewal fees, and any vacancy or inspection charges.

title: Property Management Marketing Strategies: 9 Ideas to Win More Owners
content:
## Nine strategies and claims about owner leads

| # | Strategy | Details stated on the page |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Referral system with current owners | Ask happy owners for referrals at natural moments, make it easy, and thank them every time. |
| 2 | Realtor and investor agent partnerships | Agents are asked about rentals constantly. Partner with agents who do not manage property, and refer sales back to them. |
| 3 | Tenant and vendor referral loop | Tenants may become owners, and vendors work for owners. Provide a good experience and make a simple ask so they keep the company in those conversations. |
| 4 | Review engine | Ask every happy owner and tenant for a review, reply to every review, and keep reviews recent. |
| 5 | Niche brand and clear positioning | Choose who the company serves best and say it plainly; owners remember a company that is clearly for them. |
| 6 | Trust-building website | Show who the company is, why it does this work, real reviews, and one clear next step. |
| 7 | Local search basics | Maintain a complete local business profile, steady reviews, and pages answering real owner questions to help local owners find the company. |
| 8 | Content and video owners search for | Answer owners’ pre-hiring questions through short videos, articles, or a podcast. |
| 9 | Speed to lead and a sales process | Follow up quickly, assign one person to own the lead, and make the first call a conversation. |

## Claims about which sources produce the best owner leads

- The page does **not** provide numerical lead-volume, conversion-rate, or ROI comparisons among marketing sources.
- It recommends starting with **referrals, reviews, and a clear niche message**, then adding channels one at a time.
- It says to track which channels bring owners who sign and invest more in those channels.
- For a **new company**, the suggested first three are a referral system, review engine, and trust-building website.
- For a company **stuck at a plateau**, the suggested priorities are fixing trust leaks, realtor partnerships, and speed to lead.
- For a company **scaling with a team**, the suggested priorities are niche branding and content/video, followed by paid channels on top of what already works.
- Paid ads should come **after trust leaks are fixed**, so the company is not paying for leads it cannot sign.
- Social media can support trust by showing who the company is and how it works, but the page says it is **rarely the main lead source on its own**; it recommends pairing it with referrals and reviews.
- Low-cost ideas identified are asking current owners for referrals, partnering with local agents, asking happy clients for reviews, and completing the local business profile; these cost more time than money.
- For marketing to real estate investors, the page recommends partnering with investor-friendly agents, showing clear reporting and investor-relevant numbers, and positioning the company for the types of properties those investors buy.

## Sales advice and related claims

- Follow up with leads quickly and make sure one person is responsible for each lead.
- Make the first call a conversation, not a pitch.
- Track which channels bring owners who sign.
- The page identifies six trust leaks that can cause leads to go quiet:
  - **Branding:** the name and look say “small” or “same as everyone else.”
  - **Reviews:** too few, too old, or unanswered.
  - **Website:** looks like every other property-management site and does not establish trust.
  - **Pricing:** designed to win on price, attracting price shoppers.
  - **Purpose:** does not explain why the company does this or how it is different.
  - **Sales:** the first call is a pitch instead of a conversation.
- The page advises fixing these leaks before adding strategies; fixing them makes every lead source work harder.
- A marketing plan should include goals for leads and signed doors, the channels to use, a time-and-money budget for each, and a simple monthly way to track results.

title: SEO for Property Management: A Local Search Guide
content:
## Page mapping

- Map every important search to **exactly one page** to avoid overlap and keyword cannibalization.
- Decide which audience each page serves. Owners and renters use different search terms and need different information; mixing both audiences on one page usually serves neither.
- Group keywords by **intent**, not just wording. For example, “Property management company Austin” and “Austin property managers” belong on the same page.
- Put the target query in the page’s title tag and H1.
- Example page assignments:
  - **Owner or investor searches** such as “property management company [city]” and “rental property management”: service and city pages.
  - **Owner cost searches** such as “property management fees” and “how much do property managers charge”: a pricing page or fee guide that explains fee types and what is included; the article recommends using your own pricing.
  - **HOA or condo board searches** such as “hoa management company”: an HOA service page.
  - **Renter searches** such as “apartments for rent near me” and “[neighborhood] homes for rent”: listings and neighborhood pages.
  - **Current tenant searches** such as “[your company] portal” and “[your company] maintenance request”: a resident page with login, payment and maintenance links.
  - **Residential management**: a residential management service page.
  - **Commercial property management**: a commercial service page, if offered.
  - **Vacation rental management**: a vacation rental service page, if offered.
- Prioritize owner pages in the strongest markets first, then fee and service guides, followed by neighborhood and listing pages.
- Measure performance using owner leads from organic search, Business Profile actions, rental applications and showing requests, Search Console clicks for owner keywords by city, and review count and average rating.

## City pages and doorway-page risk

- Build city pages only for real markets where the company manages properties and can serve owners well.
- Give each city page useful local information that readers cannot get from the other pages. Suggested details include:
  - Number and types of homes managed and neighborhoods covered.
  - Local team member responsible for leasing or owner relations.
  - Local owner requirements, such as rental registration or inspection rules, with a link to the city’s own page.
  - Current listings in that city, pulled from the listings feed.
  - Reviews from owners and residents in that city.
  - Typical rent ranges, when supported by the company’s own data.
- If a city page cannot include that kind of detail, include the city in a “markets we serve” section on a broader page instead. The article says fewer, stronger pages beat dozens of thin ones.
- Google’s spam policies define doorway abuse as creating pages to rank for specific, similar search queries. The article gives “multiple domain names or pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page” as an example.
- Reusing the same template and only changing the city name across many suburbs—such as 40 suburbs—is identified as that pattern and risks doorway-page treatment.
- The FAQ recommends one city page for each market where the company actually manages properties and can add local details such as neighborhoods, listings, team and reviews.

## Google Business Profile (GBP)

- **Eligible locations:** Google lists rental or for-sale properties such as vacation homes, model homes and vacant apartments as ineligible for a profile. Staffed sales and leasing offices are eligible for verification, including an on-site leasing office staffed during its posted hours.
- A business must make in-person contact with customers during its stated hours to qualify.
- An individual rental home cannot have its own profile.
- **Service-area businesses:** Use one profile for the central office with a designated service area. The service area should extend no farther than about **2 hours of driving time** from the business.
- You can set up to **20 service areas**, by city, postal code or other area. Google does not allow setting a radius.
- Remove the address if customers are not served there. If owners or tenants visit the office, keep the address and add the service area.
- **Business name:** Use the real business name. Google does not permit unnecessary information such as service descriptions or location details in the name. The article gives “Oak Street Property Management” as an acceptable example if it is the legal or signage name, and “Best Rentals Austin” as an unacceptable addition.
- Choose the most specific primary category that describes the business. Add secondary categories only for services actually offered, such as HOA management.
- Complete all fields, including hours and holiday hours, services, a description naming the markets served, phone number and the URL of the matching site page.
- Use only one profile per real location. Do not create profiles for virtual offices or mailboxes, which are ineligible.
- Fake addresses and keyword-stuffed names are identified as risks for profile suspension. For visibility in a town without a staffed office, the article recommends a strong service page and reviews from owners there rather than a new profile.
- Google says local results are based mainly on **relevance**, **distance** and **prominence**. Prominence also depends on links to the business and the number of reviews. The article states that there is no way to pay for a better local ranking.
- Add UTM tags to the GBP website link so profile traffic can be separated in GA4.

## Schema and technical recommendations

- Add **LocalBusiness structured data** with the business name, address, phone, hours and URL.
- The article recommends testing structured data with a schema validator.
- Keep name, address and phone details consistent across the website, profile and directories; use one format everywhere and update directories when the business moves.
- Host listings on the company’s own domain where the software allows it, rather than relying only on an embedded iframe or separate vendor subdomain. The article says content inside an iframe usually does not count as the site’s page content.
- Give each available unit or property a stable URL and descriptive title, such as the address or building name, bedrooms and neighborhood.
- Keep evergreen building and neighborhood pages live after units are leased, and link individual listings back to them.
- Write unique listing descriptions rather than using identical text syndicated to every listing site.
- When a unit is leased, mark it as leased or redirect it to the building page rather than leaving a dead listing.
- Write unique titles and H1s for city and listing pages; duplicate title tags can cause pages to compete and look templated.

## Reviews

- Reviews are described as the local-ranking prominence lever a property manager can influence most directly. Google says more reviews and positive ratings can help local ranking, and helpful replies can help a business stand out.
- BrightLocal’s **2026 Local Consumer Review Survey of 1,002 US adults** reported:
  - **97%** read reviews online.
  - **89%** expect a response to reviews.
  - **80%** are likely to use a business that replies to all reviews.
  - **68%** only use businesses rated 4+ stars.
  - **45%** use AI tools for local recommendations; the article says this rose from **6% to 45% in a year**.
- Ask owners for reviews after a strong first year, a fast lease-up or a clean annual report.
- Ask residents after move-in and after maintenance requests; the article recommends asking when a request is closed quickly rather than at lease renewal.
- Reply to every positive and negative review. Keep resident details private in replies.
- Do not gate or buy reviews; ask everyone the same way.
- The article notes that a calm, specific reply explaining how an issue was handled can reassure prospective owners.
- Check review count and average rating per profile monthly.

title: Property Management Marketing Plan for Google Search Ads
content:
## Negative keywords

## Landing page recommendations

- No specific landing-page design, copy, or URL recommendations are provided.

- The page says that after an ad gets a company into an owner’s consideration set, **the website, reviews, and whoever answers the phone help win the business**.
